extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents) and parties in OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and application of USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct in an Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) disciplinary proceeding involving alleged failures to communicate, fee disclosures, cooperation with investigations, recordkeeping, and misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall: .. [k]eep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter." 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to client inquiries and repeated unfulfilled promises about completion/delivery are examples of violating this rule. The opinion lists numerous specific missed responses and promises (dates and phone/email commitments) as factual examples. Excuses such as computer problems are not sufficient when multiple alternative means of communication existed; a practitioner obliged to decline the work if he lacked resources to perform it in a timely manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty/fraud/deceit/misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to: ... [e]ngage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation." 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes false or misleading statements to clients or third parties (e.g., statements about the status of applications). Intent can be shown by actual knowledge or by reckless disregard for the truth (scienter may be established by reckless conduct). The Tribunal weighs credibility and contemporaneous evidence; where the practitioner could reasonably have believed a statement was true, Director may fail to prove violation by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication of scope and basis/rate of fee (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule: "The scope of the representation and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses for which the client will be responsible shall be communicated to the client, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after commencing the representation... Any changes in the basis or rate of the fee or expenses shall also be communicated to the client." 37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rule does not mandate a signed written agreement; oral communication is sufficient if done before or within a reasonable time after retention. Changes during representation are permitted so long as communicated to the client. Evidence of a misunderstanding or confusing engagement letter may be relevant, but the practitioner satisfies the rule if the fee basis/rate and any agreed changes were actually communicated and understood (example: confirmatory emails reflecting a flat fee and subsequent agreement to increase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate with disciplinary investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: "...a practitioner in connection with a disciplinary ... matter, shall not: ... fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation of any matter before it, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority...." 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not responding timely and fully to OED Requests for Information (RFIs) and Lack of Cooperation letters is misconduct. The Tribunal treats lack of timely, full, and direct responses as failure to cooperate; such conduct is not excused by inadvertence when timelines were known and alternative responses were available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to: ... [d]Engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice." 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to cooperate with disciplinary authorities or otherwise not abiding by procedural rules can be prejudicial to administration of justice. The opinion cites case law that conduct which undermines the spirit of court/tribunal rules falls within this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust account records & preservation (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A client's f]unds shall be kept in a separate account maintained in the state where the practitioner's office is situated ... Complete records of such account funds and other property shall be kept by the practitioner and shall be preserved for a period of five years after termination of the representation." 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must maintain complete records of client/trust accounts and preserve them for five years after representation ends. The opinion also references 11.115(f)(1) as specifying the required records (the Tribunal later evaluates compliance with required-records provisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conduct reflecting fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to: ... [e]ngage in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office." 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision is construed narrowly; conduct that violates other specific provisions cannot separately be charged under § 11.804(i). The Director in this matter did not pursue this charge further (treated as withdrawn). Precedent shows § 11.804(i) is not a catchall where other prohibitions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal requires allegations of professional misconduct to be established by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several counts were evaluated under the clear-and-convincing standard; where testimony is second-hand or lacks contemporaneous corroboration (e.g., no testimony/affidavit from an investigating Bar representative), the Director may fail to meet this burden. Credibility assessments of witnesses and documentary evidence (emails, receipts, contemporaneous records) are pivotal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on contemporaneous documentation and firsthand testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal gives substantial weight to contemporaneous emails, receipts, and firsthand testimony; absence of contemporaneous evidence or direct testimony weakens allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Director's charge based on a telephone conversation with a Bar representative was undermined because that witness did not testify and only second-hand recollection and later testimony were available. The decision repeatedly contrasts credible contemporaneous documents (confirmatory emails, receipts) with later recollections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to accept representation only if able to devote sufficient resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must decline or not accept work if he lacks the resources or ability to perform the representation in a timely and diligent manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal noted that knowing a client expected prompt work, a practitioner who is employed full-time and lacks time to perform moonlighting work should decline engagement rather than accept and then delay. Estimated drafting times and the availability of meetings were used as factual benchmarks showing the work could have been completed more promptly.
